title: How to Use Interactive Demos in Cold Email & LinkedIn Outreach | Storylane
summary: Use an interactive demo as the hook in cold email and LinkedIn sequences. Learn where to embed Storylane demos, how to read demo-open data, and how to personalize follow-ups based on what prospects clicked.
body_markdown:
Here is my honest take after years of watching outbound go stale: the highest-leverage upgrade to your cold email and LinkedIn outreach is not a cleverer subject line or a longer sequence. It is an interactive demo. Learning how to use interactive demos in cold email and LinkedIn outreach (with examples) is the difference between asking a stranger for 30 minutes and letting the product answer "is this for me?" in 90 seconds.


Plain-text prospecting is commoditized. Everyone has the same frameworks, the same "quick question" openers, the same three-touch cadence. The one thing your competitors are not doing is handing the buyer a working slice of the product inside the message itself.


> **Definition:** An interactive demo is a clickable, self-guided walkthrough of your product, captured from the real UI, that a prospect can explore in the browser without a login, a rep, or a scheduled call.


This guide focuses on the interactive demo as the asset: where it goes in an email, how to personalize it by segment, how to sequence it on LinkedIn, and how to use demo engagement data to make every follow-up feel like inside knowledge. For cold email template frameworks and subject line writing, see[Best B2B Cold Email Templates](https://www.storylane.io/blog/best-b2b-cold-email-templates) . This article is about the demo itself as the hook that earns replies and meetings.


## Why interactive demos belong in cold outreach


Cold outreach fails at one specific moment: the prospect cannot picture what you do. They read three lines of benefit language, feel nothing, and archive. A demo skips the description entirely and shows them.


One buyer put the core problem more sharply than any marketing deck ever has.


> "The problem is how can they appreciate what it even does?" - \[Product Enablement Engineer, cybersecurity\]


That is the whole game. Buyers are not lazy, they are cautious, and a wall of text gives them nothing to evaluate. An interactive demo gives them something to click, and clicking is how modern buyers decide whether you are worth a reply.


The teams doing this well treat the demo as the payload, not the decoration. The email and the LinkedIn message both exist to get the demo opened, and everything else is context.


### The "aha moment" problem: letting prospects self-qualify before a meeting


Buyers want to do their homework before they ever talk to you, and they will do it with or without your help. One sales leader described the reflex exactly.


> "But I just know it's human nature you're going to go online... If you're able to engage with the product, maybe you know, type in some AI questions. Does it do this, does it do that? What's the pricing? Answers all of my questions." - \[Director of Sales, lab software\]


When you embed a demo in the first touch, you let the prospect reach their own "aha moment" on their own time. They self-qualify. The ones who click and explore are warm before you have said a word on a call, and the ones who do not click were never going to book anyway.


This is a mercy for your calendar. You stop spending live scoping calls on people who could have disqualified themselves in a browser tab. As one buyer said about the goal of the whole motion: "We want the product to upsell itself as much as possible." - \[Product Enablement Engineer, cybersecurity\]


Self-qualification also changes the tone of the meetings you do get. Instead of a cold discovery call, you get a conversation with someone who has already seen the product and arrives with specific questions. That is a far better first call.


### Interactive demo vs. video vs. Loom vs. screenshot: when each fits


Not every visual asset is equal, and the wrong one quietly kills your reply rate. Here is how I decide, and where each format actually belongs. For a deeper split on the moving-picture options, see our take on[interactive demos vs. explainer videos](https://www.storylane.io/blog/saas-product-demo-and-explainer-videos) .


Format Best for Weakness in outreach


Interactive demo Letting a prospect click through the actual product and self-qualify Takes setup time to build the first one


Screen-recorded video Narrated overview when you need your voice and framing Passive; the viewer cannot explore what they care about


Loom A quick, human, one-to-one hello or reply Feels personal but shows no product depth


Screenshot A single teaser image inside the email body Static; answers no follow-up question the buyer has


The pattern I follow: a screenshot as the teaser inside the email, linked to the interactive demo as the real destination. Video and Loom are supporting actors for a warm reply, not the opening move. Interactivity is what earns the second click, because the prospect gets to steer.


## Before you send: one deliverability note


A demo link in a cold email is only as good as the inbox it reaches. Use a dedicated sending domain, a custom tracking domain for the link itself, one link per message, and plain anchor text. The full email setup fundamentals, including domain warm-up, subject line best practices, and cadence structure, are covered in our guide to[Best B2B Cold Email Templates](https://www.storylane.io/blog/best-b2b-cold-email-templates) . This article focuses on the demo itself as the asset that makes the email worth sending.


## How to use interactive demos in cold email


This is the section no competitor actually delivers, so we are going to be specific. The mechanics matter more than the theory, and small placement choices swing your reply rate more than another rewrite of your value prop.


The core move is simple to describe and easy to get wrong. You embed a clickable teaser, usually a screenshot or GIF, that links to the interactive demo, and you build the entire email around getting that one click. One buyer described the actual production step better than any tutorial.


> "I can generate that link that pops up with that and then I hyperlink it into an email." - \[role not captured, IT services\]


That is the whole technical lift. The judgment is in where you put it and what you say around it.


### Where to place the demo in the email (and where not to)


Place the demo teaser in the middle of the email, after one line of relevance and before your single ask. Not the first line, because a link before context reads as spam, and not buried under the signature, because no one scrolls a cold email.


Do not stack the demo alongside a calendar link, an attachment, and a P.S. offer. Competing calls to action split attention and every extra link nudges you closer to the spam folder. The demo is the ask in the first touch, or it supports the ask, but it does not fight three other links for the click.


A useful test: if you removed every line except the demo teaser and one sentence of context, would the email still make sense? If yes, you have the placement right. If no, you are decorating rather than leading.


### Personalizing the demo to the prospect's segment, persona, or use case


Generic demos convert like generic emails, which is to say barely. The teams winning here tailor the demo itself, not just the copy, to the recipient. Buyers ask for this directly.


> "I want to be able to customize demos for specialized industries or companies or something that's very personalized." - \[role not captured, software\]


You can personalize at two levels. The first is segment: build one demo per industry or persona so a healthcare CISO and a fintech RevOps lead each see a walkthrough framed around their world. The second is per-recipient variables, swapping in the prospect's name or company inside the demo environment itself.


> "For instance, the name that was there was Jane, but I can replace that with that first name variable across the demo." - \[role not captured, software\]


Seeing their own name mid-demo is a small jolt of "this is for me" that a first-name merge tag in the email body can never match. For patterns on building outreach around a named account rather than a spray, our[account-based outreach examples](https://www.storylane.io/blog/7-examples-of-account-based-marketing-done-right) are a good starting point. Match the demo to the segment first, then layer variables on top for named accounts.


### Writing the copy around the demo: context, value, single ask


Keep the email short. The demo does the heavy lifting, so the copy only has to earn the click, and long copy competes with the very asset you want opened. A tight structure that works:


1. **Context:** one line proving you know who they are and why now (a signal, a role change, a hiring trend).
2. **Value:** one line on the outcome the demo shows, not a feature list.
3. **Ask:** one line pointing at the demo teaser, phrased as a low-commitment look, not a meeting request.


Notice what is missing: no paragraph about your company mission, no bullet list of every capability, no "worth a quick chat?" pile-on. Context, value, single ask, then get out of the demo's way. For cold email template frameworks, subject line approaches, and cadence structure, see[Best B2B Cold Email Templates](https://www.storylane.io/blog/best-b2b-cold-email-templates) .


### Example: signal-anchored cold email with an embedded interactive demo


Here is a worked example anchored on a real signal, with a screenshot teaser linking to the interactive demo.


> **Subject:** onboarding + your 12 new AEs
>
>
> Hi Priya,
>
>
> Saw you added a dozen AEs this quarter. Ramping that many reps usually means the same product walkthrough gets re-explained on repeat.
>
>
> Rather than describe it, here is a 90-second interactive demo of how teams like yours cut that ramp: \[screenshot of the product → links to the demo\]
>
>
> Worth clicking through when you have a minute?
>
>
> - Madhav


Read what the demo is doing. The signal (12 new AEs) earns attention, the demo answers "what is this?" without a call, and the ask is a click, not 30 minutes. The prospect self-qualifies inside the demo, and if they explore it, my follow-up has something real to reference.


### Follow-up emails that lead with a demo snippet instead of "just bumping this"


Follow-ups are where most sequences die, because "just circling back" adds zero new value. A demo gives every follow-up a reason to exist. Instead of nagging, you show a different slice of the product each time.


If they opened the first demo, follow up on the specific part they spent time in. If they did not open it, send a different angle: a shorter demo, a different use case, a single-feature walkthrough tied to their role. Each touch carries a new piece of product, not a new apology for emailing again.


This is also where a screenshot-to-GIF teaser earns its keep. One buyer described the exact tactic of dropping motion into the message: "Where you can copy this as a GIF or gif, however you would pronounce it to put into an email as opposed to a link." - \[role not captured, IT services\]. A short animated preview in touch three can restart a dead thread better than any breakup email.


## How to use interactive demos in LinkedIn outreach


Competitors cover LinkedIn cadences to death and never once mention a demo. That is the opening. LinkedIn is where you build credibility, and a demo is the fastest way to convert that credibility into genuine product interest.


Buyers are already improvising this motion when they have no email address to work with.


> "I was thinking about sometimes the cold outreach... We're doing it in Sales Navigator and we don't necessarily have an email address and it's like posting a showpad link into a sales nav message, an inmail." - \[role not captured, IT services\]


The instinct is right, the execution is usually clumsy. Let us make it deliberate.


### Connection request to value message to demo: sequencing the touchpoints


Do not lead with the demo link on LinkedIn. The platform and the human on the other end both read an unsolicited link in a first message as spam, so you sequence into it.


The cadence I use: view the profile, send a connection request with a short, no-link note tied to a real signal, and once accepted, send a value message that opens the conversation. The demo comes on the third beat, after there is a thread and a reason for it. As one buyer put it plainly about the channel itself: "I would say, you know, do some of that, like, cold outbound style outreach, you know, message them on LinkedIn." - \[role not captured, jobs board\].


Earning the connection first is what separates this from spray-and-pray. By the time the demo link appears, you are a known contact sharing something relevant, not a stranger dropping a URL.


### Working around LinkedIn's link limits: comments, DMs, InMail, the connection request


LinkedIn rewards native engagement and tends to bury messages that read like a bare link drop, and the connection request note gives you only a short line of space, so you engineer around both. A few tactics that work:


- Keep links out of the connection request entirely; use that short note for relevance, not a URL.
- Put the demo link in a DM only after the connection is accepted, framed as a helpful share.
- With InMail, you have room and permission, so a demo link fits more naturally in the first message.
- If the algorithm is throttling link posts, drop the demo in a comment or offer to send it, letting the prospect opt in.


The point is to respect the channel's rules rather than fight them. A demo shared as a genuine "thought this would help" lands; a demo blasted into a cold connection request gets you ignored or flagged.


### Example: LinkedIn DM and InMail that share an interactive demo


Here is how the same demo travels across a DM (post-connection) and an InMail (cold-permissioned).


> **DM, after they accept your connection:** Thanks for connecting, Sam. You mentioned scaling SDR onboarding at the summit. Built a quick interactive walkthrough of how teams handle that without live demos every time: \[demo link\]. Curious if it maps to how your team runs it.


> **InMail, cold:** Hi Sam, noticed you're hiring three SDRs. Ramping new reps usually means repeating the same walkthrough endlessly. Here's a 90-second interactive demo showing the alternative: \[demo link\]. Worth a look?


Both open with a specific signal, both frame the demo as a look rather than a pitch, and both ask a light question that invites a reply. The InMail can carry the link in the first message because the format grants permission; the DM waits until you are connected.


### Using demos to help a champion sell internally


Your best LinkedIn conversations produce a champion, not a signed contract. That person now has to sell you to a buying committee you will never meet, and a demo is the asset that travels for them. One presales leader described the exact need.


> "Where I'm thinking this tool might be helpful is in a leave behind where it might be able to watch a recording of the demo and construct something interactive, maybe with an agent that I could send afterwards for them to interact with what we showed them." - \[Director of Presales, data management software\]


Give your champion an interactive leave-behind that mirrors what they saw, so they can forward it internally without you in the room. It survives the hallway conversation and the "can you send me something?" request far better than a slide deck. Better still, collect those shared demos in a single space your champion controls, which is exactly what a[digital sales room](https://www.storylane.io/blog/digital-sales-room-software) is for.


The champion described why this matters competitively: "The fact that you can do that from the actual demo I gave them and it gives them interactions that they saw during the demo. That to me is your competitive advantage." - \[Director of Presales, data management software\]. When the internal seller can hand over the real thing, your deal keeps its momentum after the call ends.


## A multichannel sequence that uses demos across email + LinkedIn


Email and LinkedIn are not two campaigns, they are one motion. Email carries the ask, LinkedIn carries the credibility, and the demo is the shared asset that ties both channels to the same story. Before you build the cadence, it helps to[build a repeatable prospecting plan](https://www.storylane.io/blog/sales-prospecting-plan-template) so the touches are deliberate rather than improvised.


The mistake is running them on separate clocks. When a prospect sees a demo teaser in an email and then a related note on LinkedIn two days later, the repetition reads as relevance, not noise. Here is a 14-day cadence with the demo touches mapped in.


### Sample 14-day email + LinkedIn sequence with demo placements


Day Channel Touch Demo role


1 LinkedIn View profile + connection request, no link None yet; earn the connection


2 Email Signal-anchored email #1 Screenshot teaser linking to segment demo


4 LinkedIn Value DM (if connected) Share the same demo as a helpful look


6 Email Follow-up #1 New angle: shorter, single-feature demo


9 LinkedIn Engage with their content, light comment None; stay visible


11 Email Follow-up #2 with GIF preview Animated snippet to restart the thread


14 Email Breakup email Leave-behind demo they can revisit anytime


Notice the demo shows up in most touches but never the same way twice. A different slice each time is what keeps a two-week sequence from feeling like nagging. The channels reinforce each other: the LinkedIn touches make the emails feel expected, and the emails give the LinkedIn notes a reason to exist.


## Examples by use case


The play changes shape depending on who you are prospecting and why. Three use cases cover most outbound, and each has a distinct demo angle.


**New-business outbound.** The prospect does not know you exist, so the demo answers "what is this and is it for me?" Lead with a segment-specific walkthrough that shows the single outcome they care about, and keep the copy to context, value, ask. This is the classic self-qualification play from the top of this guide.


**Feature adoption and expansion.** Here the account already uses you, so the demo shows a capability they are not using yet. One buyer described building outreach around the single most common question a user has: "Here's a use case that I envision is either this is a leave behind or this is something on the website where they'll say, how do I enter a sample?... How do I get a sample into the system is a very easy, simple. Almost everyone's brain is going to go to that one first." - \[Director of Sales, lab software\]. Build the demo around that one question and the expansion pitches itself.


**Re-engaging a stalled deal.** A dead thread needs a reason to reopen, and "just checking in" is not one. Send an interactive demo of whatever changed since you last spoke: a new feature, a fresh use case, a workflow tied to the objection that stalled the deal. The demo gives you a legitimate, non-needy reason to reappear in the inbox.


The through-line across all three is the same instinct one buyer voiced: let the product carry the conversation. "We want the product to upsell itself as much as possible." - \[Product Enablement Engineer, cybersecurity\].


## Measuring what works: demo-open rate vs reply rate


Measure the right thing or you will optimize the wrong one. Open rate is the metric most outbound teams still cling to, and it is the least trustworthy number you have.


Since Apple introduced Mail Privacy Protection, opens are pre-fetched by Apple's servers whether or not a human ever read the email, which inflates open rates into fiction (Apple, 2021). Reply rate is the honest headline metric, because a reply is a human choosing to respond. Everything else is diagnostic.


The advantage of demos is that they give you a layer of signal no plain-text email can: demo-specific engagement. Track these alongside reply rate, and understand what each metric tells you about the demo versus the email wrapper around it.


Metric What it tells you How to act on it


Reply rate Whether the message earned a human response Primary north star; test copy and signal against it


Demo-open rate The teaser and ask earned a click into the demo Low demo-opens mean fix the copy or placement, not the demo itself


Completion rate The demo held attention to the end Low completion means the demo is too long or the wrong angle for this segment


Time in demo Depth of genuine interest High time-in-demo is your cue to follow up now, warmly and specifically


Steps viewed Which parts of the product the prospect explored Use the specific step to personalize your next touch


### Using demo engagement data to personalize follow-ups


This is the capability that separates a demo-powered sequence from a generic cadence. When someone opens your demo, you know more than whether they clicked: you know which steps they visited, how long they spent, and where they stopped. That data is the brief for your next message.


Three patterns that work:


- **They completed the demo.** Your follow-up references the outcome at the end: "You saw how \[feature\] works. The question I get most from teams at that stage is \[X\]. Happy to answer it."
- **They dropped off halfway.** They saw enough to stay interested but not enough to self-qualify. Send a shorter, single-step version of the piece they did not reach.
- **They did not open at all.** The email wrapper failed, not the demo. Change the framing, the signal, or the segment before you retry the same asset.


This turns demo analytics from a reporting tool into a next-touch trigger. A prospect who spent three minutes on your pricing or integration step is warmer than most inbound leads. The follow-up that says "I noticed you looked at the \[integration\] section, here is how that works for teams like yours" lands differently than any "just bumping this" message ever could. ## Common mistakes to avoid


I have watched all of these sink otherwise good sequences. Avoid them and you are ahead of most outbound teams:


- **Generic, un-personalized demos.** A demo that could go to anyone converts like an email that goes to everyone. Tailor to segment first, recipient second.
- **Pitching in the first touch.** The opening move is a look, not a meeting request. Let the demo do the selling before you ask for time.
- **Too many links.** One link per email. Competing calls to action split attention and drag you toward the spam folder.
- **No clear next step.** After the demo, tell them exactly what happens next. Ambiguity kills momentum harder than a weak pitch.
- **Skipping mobile and QA checks.** Many prospects open outbound on their phone, so confirm the demo renders well on a small screen and that every interaction lands before you send. A demo that mis-times a click or displays as a sliver on mobile does more harm than no demo at all.


Most of these come down to one discipline: respect the buyer's attention. The demo is a gift of clarity, so do not wrap it in noise.

## FAQ


**Do demo links hurt deliverability?**


They can, if you are careless. A link from an unknown redirect or a naked shortener reads as risk to spam filters. Use a custom tracking domain, plain anchor text, and one link per email on a warmed, dedicated sending domain, and a demo link lands in the inbox just fine.


**Interactive demo vs. video in cold email: which is better?**


For cold outreach, an interactive demo usually wins because the prospect can explore what they care about and self-qualify. Video is passive and shows only what you chose to record. Use a short video or Loom for a personal, one-to-one reply, and lead with an interactive demo when you want the prospect to steer.


**Can I put a demo link in a LinkedIn connection request?**


No. Keep links out of the short connection request note entirely, since LinkedIn and the recipient both treat an unsolicited link as spam. Send the demo in a DM after the connection is accepted, or in an InMail where the format grants more permission.


**Where in the sequence should the demo go?**


Introduce a demo teaser in the first email, placed after one line of context and before your single ask. On LinkedIn, wait until you are connected, then share it on the second or third touch. In follow-ups, lead with a new demo angle rather than "just circling back."


**How long should an interactive demo for outreach be?**


Short. Aim for a walkthrough a busy prospect can finish in around 60 to 90 seconds, focused on one outcome or the single question they are most likely to have. If completion rate drops off, the demo is too long or off-target, so trim it to the one thing that earns the reply.
